normativeSections.xml:
JNode Types JNodes are introduced

A JNodeType matches a .

Specifically:

The forms jnode() and jnode(*) are equivalent, and match any JNode.

The first argument constrains the value of the ·jkey· property:

If there are no arguments, the default for the first argument is *.

If the first argument is an NCName, this is equivalent to writing the NCName as a string literal by adding quotation marks. For example, jnode(Status) is simply an abbreviation for jnode("Status").

If the first argument is a Constant, then it specifies a value that must match the value of the ·jkey· property of the JNode, according to the rules of the fn:atomic-equal function.

If the first argument is (), then the ·jkey· property must be absent: that is, the JNode must be the root of a JTree.

If the first argument is *, then the ·jkey· property may take any value, or may be absent.

The second argument, if present, constrains the ·jvalue· property of the JNode:

If the argument is omitted then there are no constraints on the ·jvalue· property

If the argument is a sequence type, then the value of the ·jvalue· property of the JNode must match this sequence type.

For example:

jnode(*) matches any JNode.

jnode(()) matches a JNode that is the root of a JTree.

jnode((), map(*)) matches a JNode that is the root of a JTree and whose ·jvalue· property is an instance of map(*).

jnode("first name") matches any JNode whose ·jkey· property is the string "first name".

jnode(surname) matches any JNode whose ·jkey· property is the string "surname".

jnode("first name", xs:string) matches any JNode whose ·jkey· property is the string "first name" and whose ·jvalue· property is an instance of xs:string.

jnode(*, array(xs:integer)) matches any JNode whose ·jvalue· property is an array of integers.

Effect of / with JNodes

This section is non-normative.

The effect of a path expression such as E1/E2/E3/... when E1 selects a sequence of JNodes is very similar to the effect when E1 selects XNodes, provided that the steps are navigational. The provisions for writing abbreviated steps, however, are somewhat different.

If the first step selects JNodes, then all subsequent steps will also select JNodes. This is achieved by the of E2, which ensures that any step that is not explicitly navigational is interpreted as defining a selection of JNodes on the child axis.

Under the , which applies where E2 is non-navigational, the value of E2 is used as a map key or array subscript to select JNodes from among the children of the context JNode.

E2 is then evaluated with an absent focus, which means that using an expression such as data(), string(), upper-case(), or jvalue() as the final step will result in a type error. Instead, such operations must use a different operator such as ! or =!>.

The steps in a path expression for searching a JTree will often be literals or simple context-free expressions that evaluate to strings for selection within a map, or integers for selection within an array. For example, in the path $booklist/$category//author/1/"last name", the first subexpression selects the root of the JTree, and the subsequent steps (with the exception of the implicit descendant-or-self::node() step implied by the // operator) are context-free expressions that evaluate to map keys or array subscripts to be selected within the child axis.

An unquoted string such as author is equivalent to the quoted string "author", and enables the path to be written more concisely when the keys are simple NCNames.

In a path that selects within an XTree, a step such as book expands to child::book, which can itself be seen as a shorthand for child::*[node-name() = #book], selecting the child element whose name is the QName #book. Similarly, when selecting within a JTree, the step book can be viewed as shorthand for child::*[jkey() = "book"], selecting the entry within a map whose key value is "book".

Another way to view the distinction between different kinds of expression acting as steps is to consider that expressions can be classified into those that depend on the focus, and those that are independent of the focus. All the expressions that are defined here as come into the first category, while all expressions with no focus dependency are available for computing key values and subscripts. This leaves expressions that depend on the focus but that are not defined as unavailable for use as steps; most of these (functions calls such as jkey()) would not be useful as steps in a path because they do not select nodes. If such a function is used as a step over a JTree, a type error will result, because under the the expression is evaluated with an absent focus. This leaves a small number of expressions such as root() which cannot be used in a path because (a) they are not classified as navigational, but (b) they depend on the focus. Calls on user-defined functions may also fall into this category. To incorporate such functions into a path, use an operator such as =>, =!>, or ! in place of the / operator (while bearing in mind that the operator precedence may be different).

JNode Patterns JNode Patterns are new in 4.0.

A JNodePattern matches JNodes. It has three parts:

The JNodePatternSelector defines the required value of the ·jkey· property of the JNode.

The SequencePattern matches the ·jvalue· property of the JNode.

The optional list of zero or more predicates defines further conditions that the JNode must satisfy.

Here are some examples of JNode patterns:

Matching JNodes

The pattern jnode("code", atomic(xs:string)) matches any JNode whose ·jkey· is the string "code" and whose ·jvalue· is an instance of xs:string.

The pattern jnode("date of birth", atomic(xs:date)) matches any JNode whose ·jkey· is the string "date of birth" and whose ·jvalue· is an instance of xs:date.

The pattern jnode(*, array(.*)) matches any JNode whose ·jvalue· is an array, regardless of its ·jkey· property.

The pattern jnode(*, {"Author", "Title", *})[ancestor::books] matches any JNode whose ·jvalue· is a map (or record) that includes the keys "Author" and "Title", provided it has an ancestor with the ·jkey· value "books".

The pattern jnode(*, {"Author": .[.="Dickens"]), "Title", *)) matches any JNode whose ·jvalue· is a map having an Author entry with the value "Dickens", a Title entry with any value, and optionally other entries.

The pattern jnode(*, .*)[jkey() = current-date()] matches any JNode whose ·jkey· property is an xs:date value equal to the current date. The comparison uses the implicit timezone from the dynamic context. The rules for error handling in patterns ensure that any JNode whose ·jkey· value is of a type other than xs:date does not match, because evaluation of the predicate raises an error.

More specifically, a JNode J matches the pattern if all the following conditions are satisfied:

One of the following conditions is satisfied:

The JNodePatternSelector is *; The JNodePatternSelector is a Constant. and J has a ·jkey· property that is equal to the value of the constant (evaluated as an XPath expression) under the rules of the fn:atomic-equal function. The ·jvalue· property of J matches the SequencePattern.

All the predicates are satisfied. The predicates are evaluated against the item J in the same way as for a predicate pattern.

Default Priority for JNode Patterns JNode patterns are new in 4.0.

The default priority of a JNode pattern (see ) is determined by the first of the following rules that applies:

If the pattern contains at least one predicate, then +1.

Otherwise, the maximum of the following:

If the JNodeSelectorPattern is a constant, then +0.5

If the SequencePattern is empty-sequence(), then +0.5

If the SequencePattern comprises a Pattern and an optional OccurrenceIndicator, then the default priority of that Pattern.

For example:

The default priority of the pattern jnode(*, item()*) is −0.5.

The default priority of the pattern jnode(*, array(~xs:integer)) is +0.25.

The default priority of the pattern jnode("dimensions", array(~xs:integer)) is +0.5.

The default priority of the pattern jnode("dimensions", array(~xs:integer))[../"shape"] is +1.
